content: Epilepsy is a neurological disorder characterized by recurrent, unprovoked seizures. Approximately two-thirds of these seizures can be effectively managed with antiepileptic medications. However, for patients whose seizures are not adequately controlled by medication, surgical intervention may either completely eliminate or significantly reduce the frequency of disabling seizures. A critical aspect of epilepsy surgery is the accurate localization of the epileptogenic zone, which is the specific area of the brain where seizures originate. Despite advancements, the process of identifying these zones remains imperfect, and researchers are exploring new tools to enhance the precision of this localization. One such tool under investigation is the use of pathological high-frequency oscillations (HFOs) recorded from the brain. The primary objective of this research was to evaluate whether the use of HFOs could improve the outcomes of epilepsy surgery by aiding in the more accurate identification of epileptogenic areas. To achieve this, a systematic search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Epilepsy Group Specialized Register, MEDLINE, CINAHL Plus, Web of Science, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, with the most recent search completed on July 25, 2016. The inclusion criteria for the studies were as follows: they had to report on epilepsy surgery outcomes for a minimum follow-up period of six months and must have utilized HFOs as part of the decision-making process for surgical planning. The primary outcome measure was the Engel Class Outcome System, which categorizes postsurgical seizure outcomes into four classes: class I (no disabling seizures), class II (rare disabling seizures), class III (worthwhile improvement), and class IV (no worthwhile improvement). Secondary outcomes included the responder rate, the International League Against Epilepsy (ILAE) epilepsy surgery outcome classification, the frequency of adverse events, and quality of life measures. The intention was to analyze these outcomes using a fixed-effect model meta-analysis of aggregated data. Two studies, encompassing a total of 11 participants, met the inclusion criteria. Both studies were small, non-randomized trials that lacked control groups and blinding, resulting in very low-quality evidence. These studies prospectively utilized ictal HFOs to guide epilepsy surgery decision-making. Postsurgical outcomes, assessed over a follow-up period ranging from 12 to 38 months (mean follow-up of 23.4 months), revealed that six participants achieved Engel class I outcomes (seizure freedom), two participants had Engel class II outcomes (rare disabling seizures), and three participants experienced Engel class III outcomes (worthwhile improvement). No adverse effects were reported in either study. However, neither study included a comparison of surgical outcomes guided by HFOs versus outcomes guided without the use of HFOs. In conclusion, the current evidence is insufficient to draw reliable conclusions regarding the efficacy of using HFOs in the decision-making process for epilepsy surgery. Further high-quality, randomized controlled trials are necessary to determine whether HFOs can significantly improve surgical outcomes for patients with epilepsy.
